Personagem-Jornada

De: Lê Financial Times, The Economist e livros técnicos em inglês com facilidade — a base está lá. Mas depois de 15 a 20 anos sem falar, trava na hora de defender uma posição numa reunião técnica de risco, mistura os tempos verbais e nunca praticou a escrita. Sente que o inglês profissional que precisa DIZER não acompanha o que consegue LER.

Para: Conduz uma reunião de risco em inglês com segurança — apresenta o papel dele, explica o que a equipe faz, defende e debate posições com o Banco Central e com bancos parceiros internacionais, e escreve e-mails profissionais claros. Do ler ao falar, sob pressão real.

Promessa Transformadora

De travar na fala a debater posições de risco em inglês com naturalidade. O desafio do Sergio não é começar do zero — o vocabulário técnico e a compreensão de leitura já existem. É reativar a fala e a escuta sob pressão profissional: acessar a estrutura certa na hora, responder sem hesitar a um regulador ou a um banco parceiro, e escrever com precisão. Cada aula usa o mundo dele — XP, exposições, comitê de risco, Banco Central, bancos internacionais — para que o inglês ativo alcance o passivo.

Forças
  • Leitura técnica avançada (Financial Times, The Economist, livros do setor)
  • Vocabulário de risco e finanças já consolidado no repertório passivo
  • Contexto profissional riquíssimo: XP, Banco Central, bancos parceiros globais
  • Motivação clara e urgente — a dor é concreta e semanal (reuniões de risco)
  • Maturidade e disciplina: 14 anos de mercado (Itaú + gestora) antes da XP
Pontos de Melhoria
  • Fluência oral — enferrujada por 15-20 anos sem uso ativo
  • Escuta em tempo real com sotaques não nativos (parceiros internacionais)
  • Mistura de tempos verbais (present simple x continuous x perfect)
  • Escrita profissional nunca praticada (e-mails, relatórios)
  • Acesso rápido à estrutura certa sob pressão de reunião

Metodologia

1. Do Passivo ao Ativo

O Sergio já LÊ o vocabulário de risco. Cada aula transforma esse conhecimento passivo em fala e escuta ativas, com muita produção oral sobre o trabalho real dele.

2. Contexto Real de Risco & Finanças

Todo conteúdo usa o mundo dele: comitê de risco, exposições, Banco Central, bancos parceiros. Ele pratica exatamente as reuniões que vai conduzir.

3. Fluência Sob Pressão

Role-plays graduados (guided → semi-free → free) recriam a pressão de defender uma posição diante de reguladores e parceiros, para que a estrutura certa saia na hora.

4. Ritmo Respeitoso (50+)

Mudança de atividade a cada 12-15 minutos, sem exercícios mecânicos. A experiência de 15+ anos de mercado do Sergio é recurso pedagógico central.

5. Correção Adiada e Diagnóstica

Na conversa, fluência primeiro; correção depois. O professor anota os padrões recorrentes (mistura de tempos) e devolve feedback focado, sem interromper a produção.

CCQs da Aula 1 (Concept Checking Questions)

  • "I manage financial risk" — Is that my permanent job or only today? (My permanent job — present simple.)
  • "Right now, I am reviewing the report" — Is the report finished or in progress now? (In progress, right now — present continuous.)
  • Exposure — Is it money we have already lost, or money we could lose? (Money we COULD lose.)
  • Regulator — Is the Central Bank a client or a regulator? (A regulator — it controls the rules.)
  • To mitigate — Do you mitigate a risk to make it bigger or smaller? (Smaller — less serious.)
  • "I am knowing the rules" — Is this correct? (No — "know" is a stative verb: "I know the rules.")

Lesson 01 -- Pre-class

Back in the Room -- Who Is Sergio?

Reactivating your spoken English at the risk desk. Key words: risk, exposure, regulator, compliance, stakeholder, to assess, to mitigate, deadline, on track, report, partner bank, limit. Structure: present simple (your role and routine) vs present continuous (what you are working on right now).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Risk -- the chance that something bad or uncertain will happen
"My job is to measure financial risk at XP."
Exposure -- the amount of money a company could lose if things go wrong
"We are reviewing our exposure to the market this week."
Regulator -- an official body that controls an industry, like the Central Bank
"The regulator asks for a report every quarter."
Compliance -- following the rules and laws set by regulators
"Compliance is a big part of our daily work."
Stakeholder -- a person or group with an interest in company decisions
"Every stakeholder wants a clear view of the numbers."
To assess -- to look at something carefully and judge its level
"We assess the risk of each position every week."
To mitigate -- to make a risk or problem less serious
"We always try to mitigate the biggest exposures first."
Deadline -- the latest time by which something must be finished
"The deadline for the report is Friday."
On track -- going well and likely to finish on time
"The project is on track for this quarter."
Report -- a document that presents information and numbers
"I am preparing the market risk report right now."
Partner bank -- another bank that works together with your company
"Rachel works at our partner bank in London."
Limit -- the maximum amount that is allowed
"The committee is setting new exposure limits this month."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Sergio is a risk manager at XP. He manages financial risk and works with the regulator and international partner banks. "I assess and mitigate our exposure every week," he says. Every Monday, the risk committee meets at nine o'clock to review the report. This is his routine. But right now, things are busy. This week, Sergio is reviewing the new exposure limits, and he is preparing answers for the regulator. At the moment, his team is testing a new model, and the project is on track. He knows the compliance rules very well, so he feels calm before the deadline.

1. Why do we say "I assess and mitigate our exposure every week"?
A It is a routine, so we use the present simple.
B It is happening only right now, so we use the present continuous.
C It finished in the past, so we use the past simple.
2. "This week, Sergio is reviewing the new exposure limits" uses the present continuous because:
A It is his permanent job forever.
B It is in progress now, during this period.
C It is a habit he does every single day.
3. Which sentence about a state of mind is correct?
A "He is knowing the compliance rules very well."
B "He knows the compliance rules very well."
C "He know the compliance rules very well."

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Present Simple vs Present Continuous

GRAMMAR

How to separate your role and routine from what you are doing right now.

FormUseExample
Present Simple
I / we + verb (he/she + s)		Your permanent role, facts, and routine. Signal words: usually, always, every week.I manage financial risk.
Present Continuous
am / is / are + verb-ing		What is in progress right now or this period. Signal words: now, right now, this week, at the moment.I am reviewing the report.
Third person -sWith he / she / it / the team, the simple verb takes -s.The committee meets on Monday.
Stative verbsknow, need, want, understand, mean stay in the simple form, even for now: I know the rules (not "am knowing").

Lesson 02 -- Pre-class

The Quarterly Report -- What Happened Last Quarter

Reading a risk report and reporting what happened. Key words: quarter, figures, breach, loss, spike, volatility, default, provision, to downgrade, findings. Structure: the past simple (regular and irregular verbs) to narrate what happened last quarter.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Quarter -- a three-month period in a company's financial year
"The report covers the first quarter of the year."
Figures -- the numbers and amounts in a report
"The figures came back to normal in March."
Breach -- a break of a rule or an agreed limit
"We reported the breach to the regulator."
Loss -- money that a company lost during a period
"The committee recorded a small loss."
Spike -- a sudden, sharp rise in a number
"There was a spike in volatility in January."
Volatility -- how much a price moves up and down
"Market volatility rose sharply last quarter."
Default -- a failure to pay back money that is owed
"A partner bank went into default on a loan."
Provision -- money set aside to cover a possible loss
"We set aside a provision for the loss."
To downgrade -- to lower an official rating or score
"The agency did not downgrade the desk."
Findings -- the main results and conclusions of a review
"The findings of the report were clear."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Last quarter was difficult for the desk. In January, market volatility rose sharply, and several positions lost value. In February, a partner bank defaulted on a loan, and the desk recorded a small loss. The team acted fast: it assessed the exposure, set aside a provision, and reported the breach to the regulator. In March, the figures improved, and the regulator did not downgrade the desk.

1. Why do we say "volatility rose sharply"?
A It is a finished action in the past, so we use the past simple.
B It is happening right now, so we use the present continuous.
C It is a routine, so we use the present simple.
2. Which sentence about the past is correct?
A "The bank defaulted last month."
B "The bank default last month."
C "The bank was default last month."
3. How do we make the negative past of "report"?
A "We did not report the breach."
B "We did not reported the breach."
C "We not reported the breach."

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Past Simple

GRAMMAR

How to say what happened and finished in the past.

FormUseExample
Regular verbs
verb + -ed		A finished action in the past. Signal words: last quarter, in January, two days ago.We reported the breach.
Irregular verbs
new form		Same use, but the verb changes shape.rise → rose, fall → fell, set → set
Was / WereThe past of "to be" (was for I/he/she/it, were for you/we/they).The quarter was hard; the figures were high.
Did / Did notNegatives and questions use the base verb after did: we did not breach the limit; did the bank default?

Lesson 03 -- Pre-class

The Committee Decides -- Recommending Action

Reporting what the team has done and defending a recommendation in a risk committee. Key words: committee, recommend, hedge, threshold, escalate, counterparty, approve, outstanding, buffer, flag. Structure: the present perfect (have/has + past participle) for a result up to now, against the past simple for a finished time.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Committee -- a group of people who meet to make decisions together
"The committee has approved the new exposure limits."
To recommend -- to suggest an action as the best thing to do
"I recommend that we raise the capital buffer."
To hedge -- to protect a position against a possible loss
"We have hedged the exposure this week."
Threshold -- a level that triggers an action when it is crossed
"The exposure has fallen below the threshold."
To escalate -- to raise an issue to a higher level for a decision
"We have not escalated it to the board yet."
Counterparty -- the other bank or company on the other side of a deal
"The counterparty has breached the internal limit."
To approve -- to officially accept a plan or an action
"The board has approved the action plan."
Outstanding -- not yet resolved or dealt with
"The counterparty issue is still outstanding."
Buffer -- an extra amount kept aside to absorb a shock
"We have raised the capital buffer this month."
To flag -- to point out something that needs attention
"I have flagged the risk to the committee."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

This week has been busy for the desk. The counterparty has breached the internal limit twice, so the team has reviewed the exposure and has reduced the position. We have added a hedge, and the exposure has fallen below the threshold since Monday. We have not escalated the issue to the board yet, because the numbers have improved. In the committee, I have recommended a higher buffer.

1. Why do we say "the counterparty has breached the limit"?
A The action has a result that matters now, with no finished time, so we use the present perfect.
B It happened at a finished time, so we use the past simple.
C It is a routine, so we use the present simple.
2. Which sentence is correct?
A "We have added a hedge this week."
B "We have add a hedge this week."
C "We have added a hedge yesterday."
3. How do we make the negative present perfect?
A "We have not escalated it yet."
B "We have not escalate it yet."
C "We not have escalated it yet."

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Present Perfect

GRAMMAR

How to say what the team has done, with a result that matters now.

FormUseExample
Positive
have / has + past participle		A past action with a result up to now. No finished time. Signals: already, just, so far, since, for.We have reviewed the exposure.
Negative
have / has not + participle		Something not done up to now. Signal: yet.We have not escalated it yet.
Question
Have / Has + subject + participle		Ask about a result up to now.Have you reviewed the report?
Past simple, not present perfectA finished time (yesterday, last quarter, two weeks ago) always takes the past simple: we reviewed it last quarter.

Lesson 04 -- Pre-class

The Stress Test -- What Happens If

Reading a stress-test memo and talking through risk scenarios. Key words: scenario, stress test, trigger, contingency, shock, downturn, resilient, worst-case, to unwind, liquidity. Structure: the first conditional (if + present, will + verb) to say what the desk will do if the market turns.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Scenario -- a possible future situation the team plans for
"The stress test looks at a worst-case scenario."
Stress test -- a test of how a portfolio behaves under extreme pressure
"We run a stress test before every committee."
Trigger -- an event that starts an action or a consequence
"If liquidity falls below the trigger, we act."
Contingency -- a plan for a possible future problem
"We move to the contingency plan in the worst case."
Shock -- a sudden, severe change in the market
"A market shock can hit without warning."
Downturn -- a period when the market or economy gets worse
"A deep downturn is the worst-case scenario."
Resilient -- able to recover quickly from a shock
"The portfolio is resilient in the base case."
Worst-case -- the most severe possible outcome
"In the worst-case, we unwind step by step."
To unwind -- to close or reduce a position, step by step
"If liquidity falls, we unwind the weakest positions."
Liquidity -- how easily an asset can be turned into cash
"Liquidity falls fast in a deep shock."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Scenario
Stress test
Trigger
Contingency
Shock
Downturn
Resilient
Worst-case
To unwind

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The stress-test memo describes a plan. In the base case, the portfolio is resilient. But if a sudden shock hits the market, volatility will rise and liquidity will fall. If liquidity falls below the trigger, the desk will unwind the weakest positions first. If a partner bank shows stress, the team will cut the exposure and add a hedge. In the worst case, they will escalate to the committee. The finding is simple: if the team acts early, it will protect the desk.

1. Why do we say "if a shock hits" and not "if a shock will hit"?
A After "if" we use the present simple; "will" goes in the result.
B After "if" we always use "will" for the future.
C "If" is always followed by the past simple.
2. Which sentence uses the first conditional correctly?
A "If liquidity falls, we will unwind the positions."

How to say what will happen if a real future situation arrives.

PartFormExample
The condition

The resultwill + base verb...we will unwind the positions.

UseA real, likely future situation and its result — the language of risk scenarios and contingency plans.

Lesson 05 -- Pre-class

What If -- Negotiating the Hypothetical

Debating an imagined risk scenario and negotiating with a partner bank. Key words: collateral, credit line, waiver, concession, counteroffer, freeze, downside, bailout, insolvent, negotiate. Structure: the second conditional (if + past simple, ... would + verb) for an imagined situation, against the first conditional for a real plan.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Collateral -- an asset you promise to a lender as security for a deal
"If they asked for more collateral, we would offer bonds."
Credit line -- the most a bank agrees to lend you at any time
"If the bank cut our credit line, the buffer would be tight."
Waiver -- an agreement to drop a rule or requirement for a time
"If we needed a waiver on the limit, we would ask early."
Concession -- something you agree to give up to reach a deal
"If they pushed, we would offer a small concession, not a big one."
Counteroffer -- a new offer you make in reply to another offer
"If we did not like their terms, we would make a counteroffer."
To freeze -- to stop something from being used or changed
"If the bank froze our credit line, we would post more collateral."
Downside -- the possible loss or negative side of a situation
"If the downside stayed limited, we would sign the deal."
Bailout -- emergency money to rescue a bank or company
"If a partner bank asked for a bailout, the news would spread fast."
Insolvent -- unable to pay what it owes
"If a partner bank became insolvent, we would cut the exposure at once."
To negotiate -- to discuss terms in order to reach an agreement
"If the offer were unfair, we would negotiate a longer deadline."

Downside
Bailout
Insolvent
To negotiate

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Before every big negotiation, the desk runs a hypothetical. What would happen if a partner bank became insolvent overnight? If that bank froze our credit line, we would post more collateral the same day. If it asked for a concession, we would offer a small one, not a fire sale. We would never panic; instead, we would negotiate a waiver and protect the buffer. If I were the head of the committee, I would want one clear answer: if the downside grew, would we still be safe? A good counteroffer is the calm reply to a hard what-if.

1. Why do we say "If a partner bank became insolvent, we would cut the exposure"?
A It is an imagined, unlikely situation, so we use the second conditional (if + past, would).
B It is a real plan for next week, so we use the first conditional.
C It already happened, so we use the past simple.
2. Which sentence is correct?
A "If they asked for a concession, we would offer a small one."
B "If they would ask for a concession, we would offer a small one."
C "If they asked for a concession, we will offer a small one."
3. In formal English, how do we use "to be" in the imagined if-part?
A "If I were the regulator, I would ask the same."
B "If I was the regulator, I would ask the same."
C "If I am the regulator, I would ask the same."

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Second Conditional

GRAMMAR

How to talk about a situation that is only imagined, and its imagined result.

FormUseExample
Positive
If + past simple, ... would + verb		An imagined or unlikely situation and its result. Not a plan -- a "what if".If the market crashed, we would unwind.
Negative
... would not + verb		An imagined result that does not happen.We would not panic.
Question
Would + subject + verb		Ask about an imagined result.Would your committee accept it?
The verb "to be"In the imagined if-part, formal English uses were for every subject: if I were you. A real, likely plan uses the first conditional instead: if liquidity falls, we will unwind.

The Audit Report -- Reading a Formal Risk Document

Reading an internal audit report before it is submitted to the regulator. Key words: audit, deficiency, remediation, to submit, to disclose, statement, oversight, minutes, clause, to require. Structure: the passive voice (be + past participle) to read what was done, what was found, and what is required.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Audit -- an official examination of a company's accounts and controls
"The audit was completed by an external team."
Deficiency -- a weakness or fault found in a control
"Each deficiency was recorded in the report."
Remediation -- the action taken to correct a problem
"A remediation plan is required by the committee."
To submit -- to send a document formally for review
"The report was submitted to the regulator."
To disclose -- to make information official and known
"The breach must be disclosed at once."
Statement -- a formal written record of accounts or facts
"The monthly statement was submitted late."
Oversight -- official supervision by an authority
"The desk is placed under closer oversight."
Minutes -- the written record of what a meeting decided
"The minutes of the meeting were enclosed."
Clause -- a specific section or condition in a formal document
"The letter refers to clause four of the rules."
To require -- to make something necessary or mandatory
"A remediation plan is required before the next quarter."

GRAMMAR

The audit report follows a formal style. The controls were examined by the audit team, and two deficiencies were found. A limit was breached in March, and the breach was not disclosed to the committee on the same day. The monthly statement was submitted late twice. A remediation plan is required, and it must be approved by the committee. The report will be submitted to the regulator next week.

1. Why do we say "the controls were examined" and not "the audit team examined the controls"?
A The passive voice puts the focus on the action and the object, not the doer.
B The passive voice is only used for the future.

2. Which sentence is a correct passive?

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The Passive Voice

GRAMMAR

How formal reports describe what was done, found, and required — often without naming the doer.

FormStructureExample
Present passiveam / is / are + past participleA remediation plan is required.
Past passivewas / were + past participleThe report was submitted to the regulator.
The doer (optional)Add by + person only when it matters: "The controls were examined by the audit team." Often the doer is left out.
UseFormal, impersonal writing — audit reports, regulator letters, committee minutes — where the action matters more than who did it.

Past & Present -- Talking About What Changed

Reviewing a year of change on the risk desk: what happened last year and what has changed since. Key words: trend, climb, dip, steady, peak, sharp, improve, deteriorate, rebound, track record. Structure: the past simple (finished time) against the present perfect (a change up to now).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Trend -- the general direction in which something moves over time
"The trend has improved every month since March."
To climb -- to rise steadily, step by step
"Exposure climbed sharply after the market shock."
To dip -- to fall a little for a short time, then recover
"The buffer dipped in April, but it recovered fast."
Steady -- staying at about the same level; not changing much
"The trend has been steady for six months now."
Peak -- the highest point something reaches
"Exposure hit a new peak in the first quarter."
Sharp -- sudden and large
"There was a sharp fall in volatility after March."
To improve -- to become better
"The risk profile has improved a lot since March."
To deteriorate -- to become worse, step by step
"Last year the numbers deteriorated for two quarters."
To rebound -- to recover after a fall
"The trend rebounded quickly after the April dip."
Track record -- a history of how well someone or something has performed
"We have kept a clean track record with the regulator."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Trend
To climb
To dip
Steady

To deteriorate
To rebound

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Last year was a hard one for the desk. In the first quarter, exposure climbed to a new peak after a market shock, and the numbers deteriorated for two quarters. Then, in the spring, the desk cut the biggest positions. Since March, the trend has improved month by month. The limit breaches have dropped to zero this year, and so far we have kept a clean track record with the regulator. There was one dip in April, but the trend rebounded fast, and it has been steady ever since.

1. Why do we say "Exposure climbed to a new peak last year"?
A "Last year" is a finished time, so we use the past simple.
B The change reaches up to now, so we use the present perfect.
C It is a plan for next year, so we use "will".
2. Which sentence is correct?
A "Since March, the trend has improved month by month."
B "Since March, the trend improved month by month."
C "Since March, the trend improves month by month."
3. Why do we say "The breaches have dropped to zero this year"?
A "This year" is still in progress, so we use the present perfect.
B "This year" is finished, so we use the past simple.
C It is a general rule, so we use the present simple.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Past Simple vs Present Perfect

GRAMMAR

How to separate a finished time that is over from a change that reaches up to now.

FormUseExample
Past simple
verb + -ed (rose, cut, climbed)		A finished time that is over: last year, in March, in 2024, yesterday.Exposure climbed to a peak last year.
Present perfect (positive)
have / has + past participle		A change up to now, or a result still true. Words: since, so far, this year, already.The trend has improved since March.
Present perfect (negative)
have / has not + participle		Something that has not happened yet, up to now.The figures have not arrived yet.
The signalFinished time word (last year, in March) → past simple. Up-to-now word (since, so far, this year, yet, for) → present perfect. Never put last year with have.

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Agenda -- the list of topics to discuss in a meeting
"Marina sent the agenda before the meeting."
To chair -- to lead and run a meeting
"A senior manager will chair the risk committee."
Action point -- a task that someone must do after the meeting
"Each action point has an owner and a deadline."
Owner -- the person responsible for a task or action
"You are the owner of the remediation plan."
To allocate -- to give a task or time to someone
"The chair allocated ten minutes to each item."
Follow-up -- a later action to check or continue something
"The late figures need a follow-up next week."
To sign off -- to formally approve something
"The committee signed off the new control."
To recap -- to summarize the main points quickly
"Let me recap the three decisions from today."
Takeaway -- the main point to remember from a meeting
"The main takeaway is that every risk has an owner."
To brief -- to give someone the key information they need
"Sergio briefed the committee on the plan."

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Question Forms for the Meeting

How to build the questions that open, review and close a meeting. A question starts with a helper (or wh + helper), never with the subject alone.

TypeWord orderExample
Yes / No questionHelper (did / has / is) + subject + verb.Has the plan been signed off yet?

The signalNever start a question with the subject alone. Put the helper first: not "The plan has been signed off?" but "Has the plan been signed off?"

Lesson 09 -- Pre-class

Writing Professional Emails I

Writing a formal reply to a partner bank. Key words: recipient, draft, attach, regarding, inquiry, confirm, concise, formal, acknowledge, prompt. Structure: formal register and the connectors (however, therefore, in addition, regarding) that link your ideas into one clear email.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Recipient -- the person who receives an email or letter
"Always check the recipient before you send a reply."
Draft -- an early version of a text, before it is final
"I have written a first draft of the reply to the bank."
To attach -- to add a file to an email
"Please attach the exposure report to the email."
Regarding -- on the subject of; about
"I am writing regarding the limit breach last week."
Inquiry -- a formal request for information
"We received an inquiry from the partner bank about the figures."
To confirm -- to say clearly that something is true or agreed
"Could you confirm that the meeting is on Friday?"
Concise -- short and clear, with no extra words
"A good business email is polite and concise."
Formal -- official and polite in style, not casual
"Emails to the regulator must be formal."
To acknowledge -- to say you have received or noticed something
"Please acknowledge this email when it arrives."
Prompt -- quick and done without delay
"Thank you for your prompt reply."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

This morning a partner bank sent an inquiry regarding the quarterly figures. I opened my reply with the topic, and then I answered each point. I confirmed the total exposure. In addition, I attached the updated limit table. One number was still unclear; however, I explained what I could and promised the rest by Friday. The committee meets that day; therefore, a prompt, formal reply mattered. I kept it concise and closed with "I look forward to hearing from you."

1. Why does the writer use "In addition" before "I attached the updated limit table"?
A To add a second point to the first one.
B To show a contrast with the first point.
C To show the result of the first point.
2. What does "however" show in "One number was still unclear; however, I explained what I could"?
A An extra point in the same direction.
B A contrast or a problem.
C The topic of the email.
3. Why does the writer use "therefore" in "The committee meets that day; therefore, a prompt reply mattered"?
A It shows a consequence of the first idea.
B It introduces the subject of the email.
C It adds a point with no relation.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Formal Register & Connectors

GRAMMAR

How connectors link your ideas, and how a formal register keeps an email polite.

ConnectorWhat it showsExample
In addition / MoreoverAdds another point.In addition, we have updated the limits.
HoweverShows a contrast or a problem (formal "but").The control works. However, one point is open.
Therefore / As a resultShows a consequence.The figures are late; therefore, we will wait.
Register & punctuationOpen the topic with regarding ("I am writing regarding your inquiry"), use the purpose form to + verb ("I am writing to confirm..."), and soften commands ("Could you please send it?"). A connector at the start of a sentence takes a comma after it.

Lesson 10 -- Pre-class

Cause, Effect & Consequences of Risk

Reading a risk incident report and explaining the chain behind a loss. Key words: cause, effect, consequence, impact, root cause, ripple effect, contagion, knock-on effect, to amplify, fallout. Structure: cause and effect connectors (because, since, due to, so, as a result, consequently) that link a cause to its result.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Cause -- the reason something happens
"The report names the cause of the loss."
Effect -- the change that a cause produces
"The first effect was a margin call."
Consequence -- a result that follows a decision or event
"Every choice on the desk has a consequence."
Impact -- the strong effect one thing has on another
"The impact was wider than the first number."
Root cause -- the first, deepest reason behind a problem
"The root cause was a single limit breach."
Ripple effect -- a small event that spreads to affect many others
"The ripple effect was the real problem."
Contagion -- the spread of financial trouble from one market to another
"Contagion turned one loss into a market problem."
Knock-on effect -- a secondary effect caused by the first one
"The knock-on effect hit our liquidity."
To amplify -- to make an effect larger or stronger
"Panic selling can amplify a small loss."
Fallout -- the negative results that follow a bad event
"The fallout reached our liquidity by Wednesday."

The incident report tells one story. Because a position limit was not checked, the exposure grew for two hours. As a result, the loss was already large when prices moved. The first effect was a margin call. Since two partner funds held the same position, they sold together, and consequently prices fell further. This knock-on effect was a small example of contagion. Due to the speed of the fallout, the team had no time to hedge. In one line: one missed check led to a whole chain of consequences.

A "Because" comes before a full clause; "because of" and "due to" come before a noun.
B "Because" and "because of" are exactly the same and interchangeable.
C "Because" can only start a question.
2. Which connector introduces a RESULT?
A because
B as a result
C since
3. What does the report use cause-and-effect language to do?
A Show how one small error led to a chain of larger consequences.
B List the daily routine of the energy desk.
C Describe a plan for a possible future shock.

JobConnectorsExample

Lesson 11 -- Pre-class

Hedging & Probability

Answering the committee about the future without promising what you cannot promise. Key words: likely, unlikely, forecast, estimate, uncertainty, assumption, anticipate, odds, cautious, confident. Structure: modals of probability (may, might, could, must, cannot) and the degree of certainty each one carries.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Likely -- probable and expected to happen
"A rate cut is likely before the end of the year."
Unlikely -- not probable and not expected to happen
"A default is unlikely, but we still watch it every week."
Forecast -- a statement about what will probably happen
"Our forecast shows a small rise in exposure next quarter."
Estimate -- an approximate number, not an exact one
"This is only an estimate, so please treat it with care."
Uncertainty -- the state of not knowing what will happen
"There is a lot of uncertainty in the market this month."
Assumption -- something you accept as true without proof
"The model rests on one assumption about interest rates."
To anticipate -- to expect something and prepare for it
"We anticipate more volatility after the central bank meeting."
Odds -- the chance that something will happen
"The odds of a downgrade are low this year."
Cautious -- careful, because something may go wrong
"The committee prefers a cautious forecast to an optimistic one."
Confident -- sure that something is true or will happen
"I am confident about the September figure."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Likely
Unlikely
Forecast
Estimate
Uncertainty
Assumption
To anticipate
Odds
Cautious

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The committee wanted one answer: will the exposure rise in Q4? Our forecast points up, so I said the exposure is likely to rise. I was careful with the words. The number is an estimate, not a fact, and it rests on one assumption about funding costs. The limit could be crossed if the currency weakens, although a breach before September is unlikely — the odds are low. The position has not moved since Monday, so the exposure must already be near the upper band. One thing is certain: that old report cannot be right, because we closed the position in June. There is real uncertainty ahead, so we anticipate more volatility and stay cautious. I am confident about the data, not about the timing.

1. Why does the writer say the exposure "must" already be near the upper band?
A It is a deduction: the position has not moved since Monday.
B It is an obligation from the regulator.
C It is only a small possibility.
2. What does "could" show in "The limit could be crossed if the currency weakens"?
A That the writer is certain it will happen.
B That it is possible, but not certain.
C That it already happened last quarter.
3. Why does the writer use "cannot be right" about the old report?
A He is almost sure it is NOT true, because the position was closed in June.
B He is asking the committee for permission to change it.
C He thinks there is a small chance it is wrong.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Modals of Probability

GRAMMAR

One small word carries your whole level of certainty. Choose it on purpose.

ModalHow sure you areExample
must + base verbAlmost sure it IS true — a deduction from the facts you have.The loss must be from the energy desk.
may / might / could + base verbIt is possible — you are not sure either way. Use these for a future possibility, never "can".The exposure may rise next week.
cannot + base verbAlmost sure it is NOT true. Careful: "must not" means forbidden, not "impossible".That number cannot be right.
is likely / unlikely toProbability without a modal: "Exposure is likely to rise", "A breach is unlikely". After any modal, always use the base verb: it might fall — never "might to fall", never "might falls".

Lesson 12 -- Pre-class

Presenting to Stakeholders

Standing in front of the board and staying in control of the room. Key words: overview, handout, walk through, highlight, the floor, jump in, hand over, wrap up, bottom line, pace. Structure: signposting and turn-taking language -- how to open, move on, highlight, keep the floor and close.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Overview -- a short description of the main points, without the details
"I will open with a one-page overview, not with the model."
Handout -- a printed page you give people so they can follow the talk
"The handout goes out before I speak, not during."
To walk through -- to explain something step by step, from start to finish
"Let me walk you through the numbers, page by page."
To highlight -- to give special attention to one important point
"The point I want to highlight is the funding cost."
The floor -- the right to speak in a meeting
"If I lose the floor early, the second point never happens."
To jump in -- to interrupt politely in order to add something
"Sorry to jump in, but that figure changed on Friday."
To hand over -- to give the turn to speak to another person
"At the end I hand over to Marina for the credit numbers."
To wrap up -- to finish a talk with a short, clear ending
"To wrap up, the bottom line is that we need a decision."
Bottom line -- the single most important conclusion
"The bottom line is that funding costs are eating the margin."
Pace -- the speed at which you speak or move through your points
"You have twelve minutes with the board, so watch your pace."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Overview
Handout
To walk through
To highlight
The floor
To jump in
To hand over
To wrap up
Bottom line
Pace

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Thursday was my first presentation to the board, and I did not open with the model. I started by giving them a one-page overview, with the handout already on the table, closed. Then I said: let me walk you through what changed since June. After the first topic I said let me move on to the exposure. The point I wanted to highlight was the funding cost, so I slowed my pace there and repeated the number twice. A director tried to jump in after ninety seconds, but I did not lose the floor: I said let me finish this point and I will come straight back to you, and she waited. At the end I handed over to Marina for the credit numbers, and she gave the floor back to me. To wrap up, I said the bottom line in one sentence and stopped.

1. Why did the writer open with an overview instead of the model?
A Opening with the model loses the room in the first minute.
B The board asked him not to use a model at all.
C The model was not ready on Thursday morning.
2. What does "let me move on to the exposure" signal to the room?
A That he is asking the board for permission to speak.
B That he is finished with one topic and is changing to the next one.
C That he is giving the turn to another speaker.
3. Why did the writer say "let me finish this point and I will come straight back to you"?
A To keep the floor politely without ignoring the director.
B To tell the director that her question was not important.
C To hand the presentation over to the director.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Signposting & Turn-Taking

GRAMMAR

Signposts tell the room where you are and where you are going next. Each one has a fixed shape -- learn the shape, not only the words.

MomentPatternExample
Openstart by + verb-ing (never "by explain")I would like to start by giving you an overview.
Move onlet me + base verb (never "let me to move"); move on to / turning to + nounLet me move on to the exposure.
Highlightthe point I want to highlight is + noun, or is that + clauseThe point I want to highlight is the funding cost.
Take a turnSorry to jump in, but ... (to interrupt) · Let me finish this point and I will come straight back to you (to keep the floor)Sorry to jump in, but that figure changed.
Hand over & closeGive the turn with I will hand over to + person; close with To wrap up, ... and the bottom line is that + clause. One more thing: in English you ask a question -- you never "make" one.

Lesson 13 -- Pre-class

Negotiating Terms — Weighing Two Offers

Two term sheets on the table and one decision to defend, point by point. Key words: term sheet, tenor, spread, trade-off, leverage, deal-breaker, push back, settle on, benchmark, ceiling. Structure: comparatives and superlatives (tighter than, the longest, not as flexible as, far lower than).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Term sheet -- a short document listing the main conditions of a deal
"Both banks sent a term sheet before the formal contract."
Tenor -- the length of time until a loan or contract ends
"The tenor is five years, so we refinance in 2031."
Spread -- the extra cost added on top of a base interest rate
"Their spread is twenty basis points tighter than ours."
Trade-off -- something you give up in order to get something else
"A tighter spread with a shorter tenor is the trade-off."
Leverage -- the advantage that lets you ask for better terms
"We have more leverage this year, so we can ask for more."
Deal-breaker -- one condition that stops the whole deal
"The ceiling is a deal-breaker; we cannot sign with it."
To push back -- to say no politely and ask for something better
"I will push back on the ceiling, but not on the spread."
To settle on -- to finally agree on one option
"We settled on Nordbank after they raised the ceiling."
Benchmark -- a standard number used to compare offers
"Their ceiling sits far below our internal benchmark."
Ceiling -- the highest level something is allowed to reach
"The ceiling on drawdowns is two hundred million."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Term sheet
Tenor
Spread
Trade-off
Leverage
Deal-breaker
To push back
To settle on
Benchmark
Ceiling

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Two term sheets arrived on the same morning, and only one of them goes to the committee. Meridian's spread is tighter than Nordbank's, twenty basis points tighter, so on price Meridian looks like the cheaper option. Nordbank, however, offers the longest tenor of the two: five years against three. That is the trade-off. Their review clause is not as flexible as ours, and the ceiling on drawdowns sits far lower than our internal benchmark — for me, that is the deal-breaker. Our leverage is better this year than it was last year, so I will push back on the ceiling and leave the spread alone. If they raise it, that is the offer we settle on. If they do not, Meridian is the best deal on the table.

1. Why does the writer use "the longest tenor" and not "a longer tenor"?
A He is naming the top of the whole group of offers, not one side of a pair.
B He is saying the tenor became longer over time.
C He is saying the two tenors are equal.
2. What does "not as flexible as ours" tell us about their review clause?
A It is the most flexible clause of the three.
B It is less flexible than ours — the two are not equal.
C It is exactly as flexible as ours.
3. Why does the writer write "far lower than" instead of just "lower than"?
A To show that the gap is big, not small.
B To show that he is not sure about the number.
C To show that the two numbers are the same.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Comparatives & Superlatives

GRAMMAR

The comparison lives inside the adjective. Choose the shape first, and the number speaks for itself.

ShapeWhen you use itExample
short adjective + -er + thanTwo things, side by side. One syllable, or two ending in -y (easy → easier).Their spread is tighter than ours.
more + long adjective + thanSame job, three or more syllables. Never both shapes at once: "more cheaper" does not exist.Their clause is more flexible than ours.
the + -est / the most + adjectiveThe top of a group of three or more. The article the is not optional.Nordbank has the longest tenor.
(not) as + adjective + asTwo things are equal, or one falls short. It closes with as, never with "than".It is not as flexible as ours.
far / much / slightly + comparativeShow the size of the gap: far lower, much cheaper, slightly longer. Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst. A comparison always closes with than, never "that".

Practice

Lesson 14 -- Pre-class

Making the Ask at the Table

The bank has answered your three asks, and now you have to ask again -- politely enough that they can say yes. Key words: the ask, grant, grace period, arrangement fee, in return, meet halfway, hold firm, package, walk away, goodwill. Structure: polite requests and offers (could you, would you be able to, would it be possible to, I would like you to, we would be happy to).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

The ask -- the exact thing you are requesting in a negotiation
"Our ask is simple: move the ceiling to our benchmark."
To grant -- to officially agree to give what someone requested
"The committee granted an increase to one hundred and eighty million."
Grace period -- extra time before a payment or a rule starts to apply
"We asked for a six-month grace period before the first payment."
Arrangement fee -- the one-off charge a bank makes for setting up a loan
"The arrangement fee is one percent, paid on signature."
In return -- what you give back when you receive something
"We accept the fee, and in return we want the ceiling raised."
To meet halfway -- to each give up part of what you want so both sides agree
"They came up, we came down, and we met halfway."
To hold firm -- to refuse to move from your position
"On the ceiling we hold firm; everything else is open."
Package -- a set of conditions offered together, not one by one
"Look at the whole package, not at the fee alone."
To walk away -- to end the negotiation with no deal
"If the ceiling stays where it is, we walk away."
Goodwill -- the friendly credit you build with the other side over time
"Three years of goodwill is why they took our call today."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

Three asks went to Nordbank on Tuesday, and the reply came back on Wednesday night. On the grace period, the answer was yes: they granted six months before the first payment. On the ceiling they moved, but not far enough. On the arrangement fee they hold firm. So Thursday is one call with one job. Could you take the ceiling up to our benchmark? Would you be able to confirm the grace period in writing on signature day? And, if the fee is really closed, would it be possible to review it at the first anniversary instead? I would like you to put the whole package in one revised sheet before the committee meets, not three separate notes. On the fee, we would be happy to accept the one percent, and in return we need the ceiling. That is where we can meet halfway and that is the only place where we cannot. Three years of goodwill say nobody here wants to walk away over twenty basis points, so we ask well and we ask once.

1. Why is it "Could you take" and not "Could you to take"?
A Because the verb after a modal always ends in -ing.
B Because a modal like could is followed by the base verb, with no to.
C Because the sentence is a statement, not a question.
2. "Would it be possible to review it?" is used here instead of "Could you review it?" because the writer thinks that
A the request is easy and the answer is obvious.
B the request is difficult, so the most indirect shape gives the other side more room.
C the request is an order and does not need an answer.
3. What does "I would like you to put the whole package in one revised sheet" mean?
A The writer is asking the other person to do it — politely, but clearly.
B The writer is saying that he will do it himself.
C The writer is asking permission to read the sheet.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Polite Requests & Offers

GRAMMAR

The polite shape is not the weak shape. It is the shape the other side can carry to their committee and defend.

ShapeWhen you use itExample
Could you + base verb?The everyday ask. Could is a modal, so the verb stays bare: no to, no -ing.Could you raise the ceiling?
Would you be able to + base verb?Softer, when you are not sure the answer is yes. Here to belongs to able to — and the verb after it is still base.Would you be able to give us six months?
Would it be possible to + base verb?The most indirect. You use it when you know the request is difficult and you want to leave the door open.Would it be possible to drop the fee?
I would like (you) to + base verbYou state your ask instead of asking a question. Two objects, one shape: I would like you to send it, never "I would like that you send it".I would like you to send the package.
We would be happy to + base verb / If you..., we would...The offer and the trade. We would be happy to accept the fee. If you raise the ceiling, we would sign this week. Contractions in speech: I'd like, we'd be happy. Never "able to giving", never "happy accept".

Reporting What They Said

The call with the bank is over, and now the committee wants your version of it. Key words: readout, stance, claim, deny, admit, insist, reassure, paraphrase, verbatim, reiterate. Structure: reported speech (he said that, he told me that, he asked when, one step back in time).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Readout -- a short summary of what was said in a meeting or a call
"Give me the readout before I write the committee pack."
Stance -- the position a person takes and defends on an issue
"On the fee, their stance has not moved since March."
To claim -- to say something is true without giving proof
"He claimed that no client of our size had paid less."
To deny -- to say that something is not true
"He denied that the number had changed since March."
To admit -- to accept that something is true, often unwillingly
"He admitted that two hundred had been discussed."
To insist -- to say something firmly again, and not change it
"He insisted that the one percent was closed."
To reassure -- to say something that makes another person stop worrying
"He reassured me that the six months were in writing."
To paraphrase -- to say the same idea in your own words
"Paraphrase most of the call, but not that line."
Verbatim -- using exactly the same words, word for word
"I want that line verbatim, in quotation marks."
To reiterate -- to say the same point again to make it clear
"Do not reiterate the fee: we have already lost that one."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The call with Nordbank ended at half past nine, and by ten the committee wanted the readout. On the ceiling, the banker said that they could go to one hundred and ninety, but not to two hundred. Later in the call he admitted that two hundred had been discussed on his side, which is useful, because it tells us the door is not closed. On the fee, his stance did not move once. He insisted that the one percent was closed, he claimed that nobody of our size had ever paid less, and he denied that the number had changed since March. He reassured me that the six months of grace were already in writing. Then he asked when we could give him an answer, and I told him that we would come back on Monday. Two lines go into the pack verbatim, in quotation marks; the rest I paraphrase. And I will not reiterate the fee on Monday: we have lost that one, and losing it twice costs us the tone of the whole call.

1. The banker's words were "The fee is closed." Why does the report say "was closed"?
A Because the fee changed after the call.
B Because reported speech moves the verb one step back in time.
C Because "is" cannot be used after the verb "insist".
2. Why is it "I told him that we would come back" and not "I said him"?
A Because tell takes a person right after it, and say never does.
B Because say can only be used in questions.
C Because tell is more formal than say in a report.
3. His question was "When can you give me an answer?" Which report is correct?
A He asked when could we give him an answer.
B He asked when did we can give him an answer.
C He asked when we could give him an answer.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Reported Speech

GRAMMAR

Reporting is not repeating. The tense steps back one place, and the reporting verb tells the room how it was said.

ShapeWhen you use itExample
say (that) + clauseNo person after it. In English you never say someone anything.He said that the fee was closed.
tell + person + (that) + clauseTell always needs the person right after it: told me, told the committee.He told me that they would move.
one step back in timeis → was · are → were · will → would · can → could · met → had met · has met → had met."It is closed" → He said it was closed.
ask + question word + subject + verbA reported question has no inversion and no do/did. A yes/no question takes if or whether.He asked when we could sign. He asked whether we had signed.
the reporting verb carries the toneclaim, deny, admit, insist, reassure, reiterate + that + clause. A request becomes ask + person + to + base verb: he asked me to send the sheet. Time and place move too: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there. Never "he said me", never "he asked when could we sign".

Handling Objections

The committee read your readout and sent back three objections. Key words: objection, concern, address, valid, sticking point, counter, common ground, caveat, soften, take on board. Structure: concessive connectors (although, even though, though, despite, in spite of, however, while).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Objection -- a reason someone gives for not agreeing with a plan
"The memo lists three objections, not three refusals."
Concern -- a worry about a risk or a result, said out loud
"Their first concern is the size, not the price."
To address -- to deal with a question or a worry directly, not around it
"Address the size, and the rest of the deal follows."
Valid -- reasonable and based on facts, so you cannot just refuse it
"The concentration point is valid, and I will say so first."
Sticking point -- the one issue that stops an agreement from closing
"The sticking point is the concentration, not the fee."
To counter -- to answer an argument with an argument of your own
"He countered with the five-year cost of the package."
Common ground -- the part of the question that both sides already agree on
"Start from common ground: nobody wants this deal to die."
Caveat -- a condition you attach to something you accept
"We accept the fee, with one caveat: the grace period stays."
To soften -- to make a message less hard, without changing what it says
"Soften the wording, but do not soften the number."
To take on board -- to accept a point and let it change what you do next
"We took the concentration point on board and asked for a cap."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Valid

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The committee sent the memo back at eleven, and it carried three objections. The first was the size of the exposure. Although the price was the best on the table, two members were not comfortable with one hundred and eighty million placed with a single bank. The second was the arrangement fee. Even though the tenor is longer and the grace period is new, one percent still looks expensive next to the zero point seven five we paid last year. The third was timing: despite the pressure from the desk, some members wanted to wait for the quarterly numbers. The chair was clear about which one decides. It is the sticking point of the concentration, not the fee. So the plan for Wednesday is simple. I say that the concern about the size is valid and that I have taken it on board. However, I do not stop there: I counter with a cap written into the contract and a second bank for forty of the amount. I address the fee last, and I accept it with one caveat, which is that the grace period stays in writing. I will soften the wording, not the number, and I will open from the common ground: nobody in that room wants this deal to die.

1. "Although the price was the best on the table, two members were not comfortable." Why is there no "but" in the second half?
A Because the second half is a question, and questions never take "but".
B Because "although" already carries the contrast, so one turning word is enough.
C Because "but" can only be used at the beginning of a sentence.
2. The text says "despite the pressure from the desk". Why not "despite the desk pressured them"?
A Because "despite" takes a noun or an -ing form, never a subject with a verb.
B Because "despite" can only be used in the past.
C Because "despite" needs a comma before the subject.
3. "I have taken it on board. However, I do not stop there." Which sentence is also correct?
A "However I have taken it on board, I do not stop there."
B "I have taken it on board however I do not stop there."
C "Although I have taken it on board, I do not stop there."

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Concessive Connectors

GRAMMAR

A good answer to an objection has two halves that pull in opposite directions. The connector is what turns the sentence, and each connector needs a different thing after it.

ConnectorWhat comes after itExample
although · though · even thoughA subject and a verb, inside ONE sentence. Even though is the strongest of the three.Although the fee is high, we accept it.
despite · in spite ofA noun, a pronoun or an -ing form. Never a subject with a verb.Despite the fee, we accept it. Despite paying more, we accept it.
however · neverthelessA new sentence (or a semicolon) before it, and a comma after it. It is an adverb, not a conjunction.The fee is high. However, the package is the best.
while · whereasA subject and a verb, to put two facts side by side.While the fee is higher, the tenor is two years longer.
where the concession sitsFirst, with a comma: Although the fee is high, we accept it. Or second, with no comma: We accept it although the fee is high. Three errors to avoid: "although... but", "despite the fee is high", "however the fee is high, we accept it".

Who Does What -- Controls and Owners

The committee approved the deal, with one condition: a one-page map that names every control and the person behind it. Key words: control, accountable, delegate, deputy, monitor, checklist, manual, enforce, bottleneck, second line. Structure: relative clauses (who, which, that, whose, where).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Control -- a step or a check that stops a risk or catches it early
"The control that catches a breach is the daily exposure check."
Accountable -- having to answer for a result, even when somebody else does the work
"I am accountable for the limit, even when my deputy runs the check."
To delegate -- to give a task to another person, and keep the responsibility yourself
"I delegate the check, but I do not delegate the answer to the committee."
Deputy -- the person who covers the job when the owner is away
"Every control on this map has a named deputy."
To monitor -- to watch something regularly, so that you see a change early
"The team that monitors the exposure sits two desks away."
Checklist -- a written list of steps that you tick as you complete them
"The checklist that we sign every morning has nine lines."
Manual -- done by a person, not automatically by a system
"Two of these controls are manual, and that is the weak point."
To enforce -- to make sure that a rule is actually followed
"A limit that nobody enforces is not a limit."
Bottleneck -- the one slow step that holds up everything after it
"The bottleneck is the approval that only one person can give."
Second line -- the independent team that checks the work of the business
"The second line reviews the file, which is why it is not our sign-off."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Control

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The committee approved the facility on Wednesday, with one condition: a single page that names every control and the person behind it. The page has four lines. The first is the daily exposure check, which Camila Reis runs at ten every morning. It is a manual control, so we also name a deputy, and the deputy who covers her is me. The second line is the cap alert, that fires automatically the moment the exposure passes the number written into the contract; Risk Systems owns it, and no person has to remember it. The third is the sign-off of any new limit. Marina Duarte is the manager who gives it, and the desk whose limit changes cannot approve its own request. The fourth is the quarterly review by the second line, the team that checks our file and does not report to us. Two things are worth saying out loud in the room. First, I delegate the daily check, but I am the person who is accountable for it, and the checklist that we sign every morning has my name at the bottom. Second, the sign-off is the bottleneck: it is the one step that only one person can give, which is exactly why a rule nobody enforces and a limit nobody monitors are the same thing — nothing.

1. "The deputy who covers her is me." Why is it "who" and not "which"?
A Because "which" can only be used in questions.
B Because a deputy is a person, and "which" is only for things.
C Because the sentence is in the present, and "which" is only for the past.
2. The text says "the cap alert, that fires automatically". Which sentence says the same thing correctly?
A "The cap alert that it fires automatically."
B "The cap alert, which fires automatically."
C "The cap alert who fires automatically."
3. "The checklist that we sign every morning has my name at the bottom." What can you do with "that" here?
A Drop it, because the clause already has its own subject: "the checklist we sign every morning".
B Replace it with "who", because a checklist is signed by people.
C Add "it" after it, because every clause needs a subject of its own.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Relative Clauses

GRAMMAR

A control map is a set of nouns with a whole sentence inside each one. The relative pronoun is what puts it there, and it is already the subject of that inner sentence.

PronounWhat it stands forExample
whoA person. Never which for a person.The analyst who monitors the exposure.
whichA thing: a control, a report, a system. It is also the pronoun you use after a comma.The daily check, which Camila runs, closes at ten.
thatA person or a thing, but only when the clause says WHICH one you mean — and then there are no commas.The control that catches a breach on the same day.
no second subjectThe pronoun IS the subject of the inner sentence. Never repeat it with he, she or it.The control that catches the breach — never "that it catches".
drop it when it is the objectIf a new subject comes right after the pronoun, the pronoun is optional.The report (that) we send every Monday.
whose · wherewhose = possession: the desk whose limit changed. where = a place or a system: the file where the breach appears. Three errors to avoid: "the person which", "the control that it catches", "the desk that the limit changed".

Stage 1.5: Fill in the Blank

Practice

Lesson 18 -- Pre-class

The Post-mortem -- What We Would Have Done

A manual control on your map did not run for three days, and nobody lost money. Key words: post-mortem, hindsight, near miss, overlook, lapse, blameless, trace back, workaround, timeline, complacency. Structure: third conditional and past modals (would have, should have, could have, might have).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Post-mortem -- a review you hold after something goes wrong, to learn from it
"The post-mortem is on Tuesday, and the note goes to the committee first."
Hindsight -- the clear view of a mistake that you only have afterwards
"It is easy in hindsight. It was not obvious on the day."
Near miss -- something that almost went wrong, and did no damage this time
"Call it a near miss out loud, or the committee will file it and forget it."
To overlook -- to fail to notice something that was there all along
"The out-of-office was in every inbox, and everybody overlooked it."
Lapse -- a short break in a routine, when a step is simply not done
"One lapse on a Monday morning, and the number ran for three days."
Blameless -- looking at the system that failed, not at the person to punish
"This review is blameless by design: the step failed, not Camila."
To trace back -- to follow a problem to the step where it started
"We traced it back to a single line in an out-of-office message."
Workaround -- a temporary way around a problem, until the real fix arrives
"We could have used the automated alert as a workaround that week."
Timeline -- the ordered list of what happened, and at what time
"Put the timeline on the table first. Opinions come after it."
Complacency -- the comfortable feeling that stops you checking, because nothing has gone wrong yet
"A quarter of good luck is how complacency starts."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Match each word with the correct definition.

Post-mortem
Hindsight
Near miss
To overlook
Lapse

To trace back
Workaround
Timeline

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The post-mortem is on Tuesday and it is blameless by design: we look at the step that failed, never at the person to punish. The timeline is short. On Monday the daily exposure check was not run, because the owner was on a plane and the deputy had never been told. The out-of-office message was in every inbox and everybody overlooked it. The number passed the limit on Tuesday, and a trader noticed it on Wednesday afternoon, by accident. If the deputy had been told on the Friday, the check would have run on time and there would have been no breach at all. If the alert had covered the manual controls as well, we would have seen it on Monday afternoon. We should have marked that control as manual on the map we sent in June, and we should have named a deputy on the same line. We could have used the automated alert as a workaround while the check was down, and nobody thought of it, because nobody knew the check was down. We might have caught it a day earlier, but I would not promise that. It is easy to say in hindsight; it was not obvious on the day. We traced the whole thing back to one lapse: a message nobody read. And we are calling this what it is — a near miss. The market moved back on Thursday and we lost nothing, which is exactly why it is dangerous: a quarter of good luck is how complacency starts.

1. "If the deputy had been told, the check would have run on time." Did the check run on Monday?
A Yes, it ran, because the deputy was told on the Friday.
B No. The sentence describes a past that did not happen and the result it would have had.
C We do not know; the sentence is about next Monday.
2. The text says "We should have marked that control as manual". What does "should have" add here?
A It says the marking was done, and done correctly.
B It says the marking is a plan for next month.
C It says it was the right thing to do, it was not done, and the writer is taking that on his own desk.
3. Why does the text say "we might have caught it a day earlier" instead of "we would have caught it"?
A Because it was possible but not certain, and the writer cannot prove it.
B Because "might have" is the polite form of "would have" in a formal note.
C Because "would have" can only be used in questions.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The Past That Did Not Happen

GRAMMAR

A post-mortem is written almost entirely in a past that never happened. English has one structure for the result — the third conditional — and three past modals for the tone.

FormWhat it doesExample
If + had + past participle, ... would have + past participleA condition in the past that did NOT happen, and the result it would have had.If the deputy had been told, the check would have run.
where would livesOnly in the result half. The if half takes had and nothing else.If we had known... — never "if we would have known".
should haveThe right thing, not done. It carries criticism, so point it at your own desk.We should have named a deputy on that line.
could haveIt was possible and it was not done. No blame in it.We could have used the alert as a workaround.
might haveA possible result, not a certain one. The honest choice when you do not know.We might have caught it a day earlier.
two trapsAfter had comes the past participle, not the simple past: known (not "knew"), run (not "ran"), seen (not "saw"). And in speech these contract to would've, should've, could've: it sounds like "of", and the word is always have.

Lesson 19 -- Pre-class

Projections and Deadlines -- Putting a Date on It

The post-mortem ended with two changes and two dates. Now the committee wants the whole plan. Key words: projection, milestone, lead time, slippage, roll out, cut-off date, commit to, backlog, provisional, horizon. Structure: future forms (will, going to, present continuous) and the deadline prepositions by, until and within.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Projection -- a number for a future period, worked out from what you know today
"The projection for the fourth quarter is flat, on today's assumptions."
Milestone -- a fixed point in a plan where one named result has to be finished
"The first milestone is the alert going live on the risk desk."
Lead time -- the time between asking for something and having it ready
"The lead time on a change to the alert is six weeks."
Slippage -- the time a plan loses when one step finishes later than planned
"One week of slippage on the system change moves every date after it."
To roll out -- to put a change into use across a team or a system, step by step
"We are rolling the alert out desk by desk from the first of September."
Cut-off date -- the last day something is accepted for the current period
"The cut-off date for the quarterly figures is the twenty-eighth."
To commit to -- to promise a date or a result in public, so that people can hold you to it
"I will commit to the first milestone, and not to the last one."
Backlog -- the work that is waiting and has not been started yet
"The backlog on Risk Systems is eleven changes long."
Provisional -- not final, and still able to change before the real number arrives
"These figures are provisional; I am confirming them on Friday."
Horizon -- the length of time a plan or a number looks ahead
"On a twelve-month horizon the exposure is flat."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text and answer the questions.

The post-mortem is written, and the committee now wants the plan behind it. There are four milestones on one page, and the deputy line is closed already. The second one is the alert: the decision was taken last week, so we are going to roll it out desk by desk from the first of September, and the risk desk goes first. The lead time on a change to the alert is six weeks, and the backlog on Risk Systems is eleven changes long, so one week of slippage there moves every date after it. That is why I will commit to the first milestone in the room and not to the last one. The third line is the quarterly number. The cut-off date is the twenty-eighth, and the figures stay provisional until then; the confirmed version will be on the chair's desk by the twenty-ninth. On a twelve-month horizon the projection is flat, and I will say so as soon as I have the closing figures — not before. The last line is already in the diary: Internal Audit is reviewing the new alert on the fourth of November at nine.

1. "We are going to roll it out from the first of September." Why "going to" and not "will"?
A Because "will" cannot be used with a date.
B Because the decision was already taken before this conversation.
C Because the sentence is about a rollout, and a rollout always takes "going to".
2. "The confirmed version will be on the chair's desk by the twenty-ninth." What does "by" mean here?
A That it stays on the desk the whole time up to the twenty-ninth.
B That it arrives on the twenty-ninth at the latest, and it can arrive earlier.
C That it arrives exactly on the twenty-ninth and on no other day.
3. "I will say so as soon as I have the closing figures." Why is there no "will" in the second half?
A After "as soon as", "when" and "until", English keeps the present and puts the "will" in the other half.
B Because the figures are provisional, and provisional facts take the present.
C Because one sentence can only carry one verb in the future.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Future Forms

GRAMMAR

English has three everyday futures, and the one you choose tells the room how much of the plan was already decided before you opened your mouth.

FormWhen you use itExample
will + base verbA decision you make as you speak, a promise, or a prediction.I will send the confirmed number on Friday.
going to + base verbA plan already decided before this conversation, or evidence you can see now.We are going to roll it out desk by desk.
present continuousA fixed arrangement: a date, and usually a time, already in the diary.I am presenting the plan on Tuesday at nine.
by · until · withinby = not later than that day. until = the whole time up to that day. within = inside that period.It is on your desk by the twenty-ninth.
no will after when / as soon as / untilThe time half takes the present and the will lives in the other half: "I will confirm it when I have the figures" — never "when I will have". Three errors to avoid: "send it until Friday", "as soon as I will have", and "Tomorrow I go to the committee at nine".
